Report Title: Measuring AI Agents' Progress on Multi-Step Cyber Attack Scenarios
Finding: For the first time, frontier AI agents can partially solve realistic multi-stage cyberattack scenarios: Claude Opus 4.6 completed an average of 9.8 out of 32 steps on the 'The Last Ones' 32-step corporate-network range (milestones) -- a 476% improvement over GPT-4o's 1.7 steps. Performance drops sharply after step 4, where tasks require specialist reverse-engineering, cryptography, and malware-development knowledge.
Finding Quote: On “The Last Ones”, GPT-4o (August 2024) averaged 1.7 steps at 10M tokens, while Opus 4.6 (February 2026) averages 9.8.; Performance drops sharply after milestone 4, which marks the transition from reconnaissance and web exploitation to attack phases requiring specialist knowledge in reverse engineering, cryptography, and malware development.
Policy Response: UK NCSC and UK AISI published a joint follow-up blog post giving UK organizations defensive guidance, explicitly building on the March 2026 AISI multi-step cyberattack finding on Claude Opus 4.6.
Media Outlets: resultsense.com (2026-03-18); wave of April-May 2026 coverage tied to successor 'Claude Mythos Preview' eval citing Opus 4.6 as prior-best: Ars Technica, The Telegraph, The Guardian, ZDNet, the-decoder.com, CyberScoop, Computing.co.uk, Help Net Security, Forbes, Business Insider, TechPolicy.press

Report Title: Measuring AI Agents' Progress on Multi-Step Cyber Attack Scenarios
Finding: On UK AISI's 'Cooling Tower' industrial-control-system scenario, GPT-5.3-Codex's best single run reached 3 of 7 steps; separately, models across the study were found to bypass the intended attack sequence entirely by directly reverse-engineering a proprietary PLC protocol from raw network traffic alone, an emergent capability not designed into the scenario.
Finding Quote: GPT 5.3 Codex achieves the highest single-run maximum of 3 steps out of 7.; several frontier models bypassed this sequence entirely: starting from the attacker's initial position, they directly probed the proprietary protocol running on the PLCs, deducing enough of its structure from network traffic alone to call unprotected functions and read PLC memory—obtaining Step 4 without any prior exploitation
Policy Response: UPGRADE. This finding comes from the same report as UKAISI-2026-03-CYB1, and the NCSC/AISI joint blog of 2026-03-30 explicitly cites that report by title and arXiv link. The rulebook admits a source that explicitly references 'the finding, report, evaluator or specific result' - the report qualifies - and the dataset already applies exactly this logic to UKAISI-2026-04-CYB1/CYB2, where uptake was granted on an explicit reference to the evaluation rather than to the individual result. The NCSC post does not reference the Cooling Tower or PLC result specifically, and imposes no enforceable obligation, so the correct level is Non-binding policy-related uptake, not Binding. Coding it 'No policy uptake identified' while its sibling row from the same report is coded Non-binding is an internal inconsistency.
